questions.stem: A client develops sudden severe leg pain with pallor, coolness, and absent distal pulses. Which interpretation is most appropriate?
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"These findings are most consistent with a benign positional circulation change that can be observed until warmth and pulses return without urgent evaluation.","B":"These findings suggest acute limb ischemia, a vascular emergency requiring rapid recognition and urgent evaluation to preserve tissue and limb viability.","C":"These findings are most consistent with an uncomplicated muscle strain because acute musculoskeletal pain commonly causes pallor and loss of distal pulses.","D":"These findings indicate chronic venous insufficiency because venous disease typically causes sudden pulselessness, coolness, and severe ischemic pain."}}
questions.rationale: The sudden combination of severe pain, pallor, coolness, and absent pulses is characteristic of acute limb ischemia, which the 2024 multisociety guideline describes as a vascular emergency. Option B correctly identifies the condition and urgency. Option A incorrectly treats ischemic signs as a benign positional change. Option C cannot explain pallor and absent pulses as a simple muscle strain. Option D misclassifies an acute arterial emergency as chronic venous disease.
questions.source_name: AHA/ACC et al. — 2024 Guideline for the Management of Lower Extremity Peripheral Artery Disease
questions.source_detail: The guideline defines acute limb ischemia by acute hypoperfusion with findings including pain, pallor, pulselessness and coolness, and describes ALI as a vascular emergency requiring rapid recognition and emergency evaluation.

qc.qc_note: Strict final audit: max/min option-character ratio <=1.15; keyed option within 10% of distractor mean; keyed option is neither shortest nor longest; distractors manually reviewed for clinical plausibility, grammatical parallelism, and answer-cue leakage.
